subject: Economics and Business
name: Economics and Business, Levels 7 and 8
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: Economics and Business, Levels 7 and 8

points.title: Needs and wants
points.brief: Needs are things people must have to survive, such as food and shelter. Wants are things people would like but can live without.

points.title: Economic resources
points.brief: Goods and services are made from natural resources (land, water, minerals), human resources (people's work and skills) and capital resources (tools, machines and buildings).

points.title: The basic economic problem
points.brief: People's wants are unlimited but the resources to meet them are scarce, so individuals, businesses and governments must choose how to use them.

points.title: The three economic questions
points.brief: Every society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and who gets what is produced.

points.title: Opportunity cost
points.brief: The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best option given up. Spending Saturday at work means giving up time with friends, for example.

points.title: Weighing costs and benefits
points.brief: A sensible economic decision compares what an option gives (its benefits) with what it takes (its costs, including opportunity cost) and picks the one with the greatest net benefit.

points.title: Incentives
points.brief: An incentive is something that encourages a choice, such as a discount or a reward. A disincentive, such as a fine or a tax, discourages one.

points.title: What a market is
points.brief: A market is anywhere buyers and sellers come together to trade, from a farmers market to an online store or the share market.

points.title: Demand
points.brief: Demand is how much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. When the price rises, people buy less, and when it falls, they buy more.

points.title: Supply
points.brief: Supply is how much of a product sellers will offer at each price. A higher price makes selling more worthwhile, so sellers offer more.

points.title: Equilibrium price
points.brief: The market price settles where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. On a graph it is where the demand and supply curves cross.

points.title: Shortages and surpluses
points.brief: If the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than is offered and the price rises. If it is above, unsold stock builds up and the price falls.

points.title: The price mechanism
points.brief: Rising prices signal businesses to make more of a product and buyers to use less, so prices steer scarce resources to where they are most wanted.

points.title: Consumer sovereignty
points.brief: In a free market, consumers decide what gets made by what they choose to buy. Businesses that ignore what consumers want lose sales.

points.title: The purposes of business
points.brief: Businesses exist to provide goods and services people want and to make a profit for their owners. Some, such as social enterprises, also aim to solve a social or environmental problem.

points.title: Business goals
points.brief: Businesses set goals such as making a profit, growing, winning a bigger share of the market, serving customers well and acting sustainably.

points.title: Business ownership structures
points.brief: A sole trader is owned by one person, a partnership by two or more, and a company is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders. Owners of a sole trader or partnership can lose their own assets if it fails.

points.title: Goods and services businesses
points.brief: Businesses can be grouped by what they sell, goods you can touch or services done for you, and by industry, from primary (farming, mining) to secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services).

points.title: Target markets
points.brief: A target market is the group of customers a business aims to sell to, described by things such as age, income, location and interests.

points.title: Spotting a market opportunity
points.brief: A market opportunity is an unmet need or gap a business can fill. Businesses find them through market research, new technology and changes in how people live.

points.title: What an entrepreneur does
points.brief: An entrepreneur spots an opportunity, takes the risk of starting a business and brings resources together to make something new or better.

points.title: Entrepreneurship and business success
points.brief: Traits such as creativity, persistence, willingness to take risks and learning from failure help entrepreneurs turn an idea into a lasting business.

points.title: Innovation
points.brief: Innovation is a new product, service or way of working. It helps a business stand out, cut costs and keep customers.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander-owned businesses are a growing sector across many industries, often combining profit with goals for community, culture and Country, with buyers such as government able to seek them out.

points.title: Risk and reward in starting a business
points.brief: Starting a business can bring profit, independence and pride, but risks losing money and time, and many new businesses close within a few years.

points.title: Why people work
points.brief: People work for income, but also for satisfaction, purpose, skills, friendships and a sense of identity.

points.title: Wages and salaries
points.brief: A wage is paid for each hour worked, while a salary is a fixed amount for a year, paid in parts. Both are income from employment.

points.title: Other sources of income
points.brief: Australians also earn income from running a business (profit), interest on savings, dividends from shares, rent from property and government payments such as Youth Allowance.

points.title: Types of employment
points.brief: Full-time and part-time workers have regular hours and paid leave. Casual workers have no guaranteed hours or paid leave but get a higher hourly rate. Contractors work for themselves.

points.title: Paid and unpaid work
points.brief: Not all work is paid. Caring for family, housework and volunteering are unpaid but add a great deal to the community.

points.title: From making goods to providing services
points.brief: Most Australians once worked in farming or factories. Today most work in services, such as health care, education, retail and professional work.

points.title: Technology and automation
points.brief: Machines, robots and artificial intelligence take over some tasks, removing some jobs while creating others that need new skills.

points.title: The gig economy
points.brief: In the gig economy, people do short jobs through apps, such as food delivery or ride sharing. It is flexible but often lacks steady pay, leave and super.

points.title: Flexible and remote work
points.brief: More people now work from home, part-time or at flexible hours, which can help balance life and work but can blur the line between them.

points.title: The future of work
points.brief: Jobs are expected to keep changing, so skills such as problem solving, digital skills and adapting through lifelong learning will matter more.

points.title: The Australian Consumer Law
points.brief: The Australian Consumer Law protects buyers across the country. It guarantees products are safe, work as they should and match their description.

points.title: Repair, replace or refund
points.brief: If a product has a major fault, the buyer can choose a refund or replacement; for a minor fault, the seller can choose to repair it. A "no refunds" sign cannot remove these rights.

points.title: Misleading and deceptive conduct
points.brief: Businesses must not mislead consumers with false claims, fake prices or hidden fees. The ACCC and Consumer Affairs Victoria enforce the rules.

points.title: Consumer responsibilities
points.brief: Consumers should read terms before agreeing, keep receipts, use products as intended and complain through the right channels.

points.title: Ethical business behaviour
points.brief: Beyond what the law requires, ethical businesses treat workers fairly, tell the truth and care for the environment, which can win customers' trust.

points.title: Comparing before you buy
points.brief: Smart consumers compare prices and quality, use unit pricing to compare sizes, read reviews and check the full cost, including fees and delivery.

points.title: How advertising persuades
points.brief: Ads use techniques such as celebrity endorsement, limited-time offers, bandwagon appeals and influencer posts to make people want to buy.

points.title: Common financial scams
points.brief: Scams include phishing messages asking for passwords, fake online shops, fake prizes and offers of quick riches. Young people are often targeted on social media.

points.title: Spotting and avoiding scams
points.brief: Warning signs include pressure to act fast, requests for gift cards or personal details and deals too good to be true. Check with Scamwatch and never share passwords or codes.

points.title: What tax is and why we pay it
points.brief: Tax is money people and businesses must pay to government. It funds services everyone shares, such as schools, hospitals, roads and defence.

points.title: Income tax
points.brief: Income tax is taken from what people earn. Australia's system is progressive, so higher incomes pay a higher rate, and the first $18,200 a year is tax free.

points.title: The goods and services tax
points.brief: The GST is a 10 per cent tax added to most goods and services. Basic food, most health care and education are exempt.

points.title: Lodging a tax return
points.brief: Workers need a tax file number. Each year they lodge a tax return with the Australian Taxation Office, which works out whether they paid too much or too little.

points.title: How tax revenue is spent
points.brief: The biggest areas of government spending are social security and welfare, health, education and defence, along with roads and other infrastructure.

points.title: Setting financial goals
points.brief: Financial goals can be short term (new shoes), medium term (a laptop) or long term (a car or home). Clear goals with an amount and a date are easier to reach.

points.title: Making a budget
points.brief: A budget lists income and expenses so spending stays below income. Fixed expenses stay the same each time, while variable ones change.

points.title: Saving and interest
points.brief: Money saved in a bank earns interest. With compound interest, interest is earned on past interest too, so savings grow faster the longer they are left.

points.title: Debt and credit
points.brief: Borrowing through credit cards, loans or buy now pay later costs more than paying upfront when fees and interest are added, and missed payments can harm a credit record.

points.title: Questions for an investigation
points.brief: A good investigation question about an economic or business issue is focused and open, asking how or why rather than something answered by yes or no.

points.title: Checking sources
points.brief: Before using information, check who made it, when, why and whether other sources agree, to judge whether it is accurate and fair.

points.title: Reading economic graphs
points.brief: Line graphs show change over time, bar graphs compare amounts, and models such as supply and demand show how two things affect each other.

points.title: Cause and effect in economics
points.brief: Economic events have causes and effects that chain together, such as drought cutting crop supply and so raising food prices.

points.title: Analysing a response to an issue
points.brief: To judge a response to an economic or business issue, list its likely costs and benefits for each group affected and weigh them up.
